PSE II · Chapter 25

Capacitance & Dielectrics

Storing charge, storing energy

← PSE II Course

25.0 — Storing the Electric Field

In the preceding three chapters, we built a powerful framework for electrostatics. We learned how charges create electric fields (Chapter 22), how Gauss’s Law relates fields to enclosed charge (Chapter 23), and how electric potential provides a scalar energy landscape (Chapter 24). We even found that the energy stored in a configuration of charges can be expressed as energy residing in the electric field itself, with a density \(u_E = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2\).

Now we turn to a practical question: Can we build a device that deliberately creates and stores an electric field — and the energy it contains?

The answer is the capacitor, one of the most fundamental components in electrical engineering. Capacitors store energy, filter signals, smooth power supplies, trigger camera flashes, restart hearts with defibrillators, and enable the touchscreen you may be reading this on. The physics reduces to one elegant idea: two conductors, separated by a gap, with equal and opposite charges.

The earliest capacitor — the Leyden jar — was independently invented in 1745 by Ewald Georg von Kleist (1700–1748) and Pieter van Musschenbroek (1692–1761) in Leiden, Netherlands. It was simply a glass jar coated inside and outside with metal foil, yet its ability to store a powerful shock astonished the scientific world. Benjamin Franklin (1706–1790) later concluded that the charge resided not in the water inside the jar, but on the glass surfaces — shifting attention to the geometry of the conductors and the material between them.

“I would like to tell you about a new but terrible experiment, which I advise you never to try yourself… I felt myself struck in my arms, shoulders, and breast so that I lost my breath, and it was two days before I recovered from the effects of the blow and the terror.” — Pieter van Musschenbroek, 1746

*Personal note: Capacitance unites the three pillars we’ve built: Gauss’s Law gives the field, integrating gives the potential, and the stored energy is the field energy over the volume. This chapter bridges “field theory” and “circuit theory.”

25.1 — Definition of Capacitance

A capacitor consists of two conductors (called plates) carrying charges of equal magnitude and opposite sign. When we say a capacitor “has charge \(Q\),” we mean one plate carries \(+Q\) and the other carries \(-Q\). The net charge is zero — what matters is the separation of charge. When connected to a battery, electrons flow until an electric field is established between the plates.

The Definition

Capacitance \(C\) is defined as the ratio of the magnitude of the charge on either conductor to the magnitude of the potential difference between them:

\[C \equiv \frac{Q}{\Delta V} \qquad \text{or equivalently} \qquad Q = C\Delta V\]

where \(Q\) is the charge on either plate (C), \(\Delta V\) is the potential difference (V), and \(C\) is the capacitance (F). The SI unit is the farad (F), named after Michael Faraday: \(1\ \text{F} = 1\ \text{C/V}\).

A farad is enormous. Typical capacitors are measured in picofarads (\(\text{pF} = 10^{-12}\ \text{F}\)), nanofarads (\(\text{nF} = 10^{-9}\ \text{F}\)), or microfarads (\(\mu\text{F} = 10^{-6}\ \text{F}\)). A 1 F capacitor charged to 1 V stores \(6.24 \times 10^{18}\) electrons. Supercapacitors in hybrid vehicles can reach thousands of farads.

Capacitance depends only on the geometry of the conductors and the material between them — not on \(Q\) or \(\Delta V\). Doubling the voltage doubles the charge, but the ratio \(Q/\Delta V\) stays the same. Capacitance is a property of the device, not of the charge stored on it.

*Personal note: Students often confuse capacitance with charge. A large capacitance means lots of charge per volt. A swimming pool and a drinking glass can both be full, but the pool holds more water per inch of depth.

25.2 — Calculating Capacitance: The Parallel-Plate Capacitor

General Strategy

To find the capacitance of any conductor geometry: (1) assume charge \(\pm Q\) on the conductors, (2) find \(\vec{E}\) via Gauss’s Law, (3) integrate for \(\Delta V = -\int \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{s}\), and (4) divide: \(C = Q/\Delta V\). The charge \(Q\) always cancels, confirming capacitance depends only on geometry.

The Parallel-Plate Capacitor

The simplest and most important capacitor consists of two parallel conducting plates, each with area \(A\), separated by a distance \(d\).

Step 1: Surface charge density: \(\sigma = Q/A\).

Step 2: From Gauss’s Law (Ch. 23), the uniform field between the plates: \(E = \sigma/\varepsilon_0 = Q/(\varepsilon_0 A)\)

Step 3: Potential difference: \(\Delta V = Ed = Qd/(\varepsilon_0 A)\)

Step 4: Capacitance:

\[\boxed{C = \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}}\]

Physical interpretation: Capacitance increases with plate area \(A\) (more room for charges) and increases as plates get closer (each plate’s field more strongly attracts charge onto the opposing plate).

Example: A Typical Parallel-Plate Capacitor

Square plates with \(\ell = 10.0\) cm, separation \(d = 1.00\) mm:

\[C = \frac{(8.854 \times 10^{-12})(0.100)^2}{1.00 \times 10^{-3}} = 88.5\ \text{pF}\]

Only 88.5 pF despite 4-inch-square plates at 1 mm spacing — this is why practical capacitors use dielectrics and rolled-up plates.

25.3 — Capacitance of Other Geometries

The same strategy — Gauss’s Law for \(\vec{E}\), integrate for \(\Delta V\), divide — works for any geometry with sufficient symmetry. We already applied Gauss’s Law to cylindrical and spherical geometries in Chapter 23 and integrated those fields in Chapter 24. Here we collect the results.

The cylindrical capacitor (inner radius \(a\), outer radius \(b\), length \(\ell\)) describes every coaxial cable used for TV, internet, and RF signals:

\[\boxed{C = \frac{\ell}{2k_e \ln(b/a)}} \qquad \frac{C}{\ell} = \frac{2\pi\varepsilon_0}{\ln(b/a)}\]

The spherical capacitor (inner sphere radius \(a\), outer shell radius \(b\)):

\[\boxed{C = \frac{ab}{k_e(b - a)}}\]

Limiting case — the isolated sphere: As \(b \to \infty\): \(C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 a\). For Earth (\(a = 6.37 \times 10^6\) m): \(C = 710\ \mu\text{F}\) — even a planet has less than a millifarad!

Geometry Capacitance Key Parameter
Parallel Plate \(C = \varepsilon_0 A/d\) Area \(A\), separation \(d\)
Cylindrical \(C = \ell/[2k_e \ln(b/a)]\) Length \(\ell\), radii \(a\), \(b\)
Spherical \(C = ab/[k_e(b-a)]\) Radii \(a\), \(b\)
Isolated Sphere \(C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 a\) Radius \(a\)

In every case, capacitance depends only on geometry and \(\varepsilon_0\) — never on \(Q\) or \(\Delta V\).

25.4 — Combinations of Capacitors

In practical circuits, capacitors are combined in series and parallel to achieve desired capacitance values and voltage ratings. The combination rules follow the same pattern as springs in Physics I — not resistors (which combine the opposite way, as we’ll see in Chapter 27).

Parallel Combination

Two capacitors are in parallel when the same \(\Delta V\) appears across both.

Same voltage, charges add: \(Q_\text{tot} = C_1 \Delta V + C_2 \Delta V = (C_1 + C_2)\Delta V\)

\[\boxed{C_\text{eq} = C_1 + C_2 + C_3 + \cdots \quad (\text{parallel})}\]

Parallel capacitors effectively increase total plate area. \(C_\text{eq}\) is always larger than the largest individual.

Series Combination

Two capacitors are in series when connected end-to-end, forcing the same charge \(Q\) on both. (The isolated conductor between them has no path for charge to enter or leave.)

Same charge, voltages add: \(\Delta V_\text{tot} = Q/C_1 + Q/C_2\)

\[\boxed{\frac{1}{C_\text{eq}} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} + \frac{1}{C_3} + \cdots \quad (\text{series})}\]

Series capacitors effectively increase plate separation. \(C_\text{eq}\) is always smaller than the smallest individual.

Series vs. Parallel at a Glance

Property Parallel Series
Same quantity \(\Delta V\) \(Q\)
Additive quantity \(Q_\text{tot} = Q_1 + Q_2\) \(\Delta V_\text{tot} = \Delta V_1 + \Delta V_2\)
Equivalent rule \(C_\text{eq} = C_1 + C_2\) \(1/C_\text{eq} = 1/C_1 + 1/C_2\)
Effect on \(C_\text{eq}\) Larger than any individual Smaller than any individual

Example: Mixed Combination

\(C_1 = 4.00\ \mu\text{F}\), \(C_2 = 6.00\ \mu\text{F}\), \(C_3 = 2.00\ \mu\text{F}\), \(C_4 = 8.00\ \mu\text{F}\), \(\Delta V = 12.0\) V. \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) in series; that pair in parallel with \(C_4\); the combination in series with \(C_3\).

Step 1: \(C_1\), \(C_2\) in series: \(1/C_{12} = 1/4.00 + 1/6.00 = 5/12 \Rightarrow C_{12} = 2.40\ \mu\text{F}\)

Step 2: \(C_{12} \| C_4\): \(C_{124} = 2.40 + 8.00 = 10.4\ \mu\text{F}\)

Step 3: \(C_{124}\) in series with \(C_3\): \(1/C_\text{eq} = 1/10.4 + 1/2.00 \Rightarrow C_\text{eq} = 1.68\ \mu\text{F}\)

Energy: \(U = \frac{1}{2}(1.68 \times 10^{-6})(12.0)^2 = 121\ \mu\text{J}\)

25.5 — Energy Stored in a Charged Capacitor

When we charge a capacitor, the battery does work against the growing field. At intermediate charge \(q\), the work to transfer \(dq\) more is \(dW = (q/C)\, dq\). Integrating:

\[U = \int_0^Q \frac{q}{C}\,dq = \frac{Q^2}{2C}\]

Graphically, \(\Delta V\) rises linearly with \(q\) (slope \(1/C\)), and the total work is the area of the triangle under the line:

\[\boxed{U = \frac{Q^2}{2C} = \frac{1}{2}C(\Delta V)^2 = \frac{1}{2}Q\Delta V}\]

All three forms are equivalent via \(Q = C\Delta V\). The factor of \(\frac{1}{2}\) arises because the average voltage during charging is \(\Delta V/2\) — geometrically, a triangle has half the area of the enclosing rectangle. Use \(\frac{1}{2}C(\Delta V)^2\) when voltage is known (battery connected); \(Q^2/(2C)\) when charge is known (battery disconnected).

Physics I Analogy

Spring (Physics I) Capacitor (This Chapter)
\(U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2\) \(U = \frac{1}{2}C(\Delta V)^2\)
Spring constant \(k\) Capacitance \(C\)
Displacement \(x\) Voltage \(\Delta V\)
Force \(F = kx\) Charge \(Q = C\Delta V\)

A capacitor is the electrical analog of a spring — energy proportional to the square of the “displacement.”

Example: Energy in a Defibrillator

A defibrillator has \(C = 32.0\ \mu\text{F}\) charged to \(5000\) V: \(U = \frac{1}{2}(32.0 \times 10^{-6})(5000)^2 = 400\ \text{J}\) — released in milliseconds, a power output of ~\(10^5\) W.

Energy Density

The energy resides in the electric field itself. For parallel plates (volume \(= Ad\)), using \(C = \varepsilon_0 A/d\) and \(\Delta V = Ed\):

\[U = \frac{1}{2}\frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}(Ed)^2 = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2 (Ad) \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \boxed{u_E = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2}\]

Although derived for parallel plates, this is completely general — wherever there is an electric field, there is stored energy.

*Personal note: This confirms Chapter 24’s result — the field carries real energy. This becomes central when we study electromagnetic waves propagating through empty space.

25.6 — Capacitors with Dielectrics

In 1837, Michael Faraday discovered that inserting a nonconducting material — a dielectric — between capacitor plates increases the capacitance. Charge a capacitor to \(\Delta V_0\), disconnect the battery (fixing \(Q\)), insert a dielectric: the voltage drops to \(\Delta V = \Delta V_0/\kappa\), where \(\kappa\) is the dielectric constant (\(\kappa \geq 1\)). Since \(Q\) is unchanged:

\[\boxed{C = \kappa C_0} \qquad \text{For parallel plates:} \qquad \boxed{C = \kappa \frac{\varepsilon_0 A}{d}}\]

Dielectric Constants of Common Materials

Material \(\kappa\) Dielectric Strength (\(10^6\) V/m)
Vacuum 1.000 00 —
Air 1.000 59 3
Paper 3.7 16
Glass (Pyrex) 5.6 14
Teflon 2.1 60
Strontium titanate 233 8
Water 80 —

Why Does a Dielectric Increase Capacitance?

The explanation is polarization. In an external field, polar molecules align their permanent dipoles and nonpolar molecules develop induced dipoles. The aligned dipoles create a field opposing the external field, reducing the net field to \(E = E_0/\kappa\). A weaker field means smaller \(\Delta V\) for the same \(Q\), so \(C\) increases. We define permittivity \(\varepsilon = \kappa\varepsilon_0\) so that \(C = \varepsilon A/d\).

Two Important Scenarios

Quantity Battery Connected (constant \(\Delta V\)) Battery Disconnected (constant \(Q\))
Capacitance \(C\) Increases by \(\kappa\) Increases by \(\kappa\)
Charge \(Q\) Increases by \(\kappa\) Same
Voltage \(\Delta V\) Same Decreases by \(\kappa\)
Energy \(U\) Increases by \(\kappa\) Decreases by \(\kappa\)

When battery-connected, the battery supplies extra energy. When disconnected, the “missing” energy was converted to work pulling the dielectric into the gap.

Dielectric Strength and Breakdown

Every dielectric has a maximum field before dielectric breakdown — sudden conduction (sparks, lightning). \(\Delta V_\text{max} = E_\text{max} \cdot d\). Dielectrics serve a dual purpose: increase capacitance and raise maximum voltage.

Example: Inserting a Dielectric

\(C_0 = 100\ \text{pF}\), \(\Delta V_0 = 50.0\) V, battery disconnected, \(\kappa = 5.0\) inserted.

(A) \(C = \kappa C_0 = 500\ \text{pF}\). (B) \(Q = 5.00\ \text{nC}\) (constant), \(\Delta V = Q/C = 10.0\ \text{V}\). (C) \(U_0 = 125\ \text{nJ}\), \(U = 25.0\ \text{nJ}\), \(U/U_0 = 1/\kappa\).

Electric Dipoles in Electric Fields

For a dipole \(\vec{p} = q\vec{d}\) in a uniform field \(\vec{E}\), the forces create a torque aligning the dipole with the field, and an associated potential energy:

\[\vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E} \qquad \qquad U = -\vec{p} \cdot \vec{E} = -pE\cos\theta\]

Minimum energy (stable) when \(\vec{p} \parallel \vec{E}\); maximum when antiparallel. This is why dielectrics are pulled into strong-field regions.

*These results reappear for magnetic dipoles — same math, different symbols.

25.7 — Applications of Capacitors

Energy storage: Capacitors release energy much faster than batteries — camera flashes, defibrillators, pulsed lasers, and particle accelerators all rely on capacitor banks.

Capacitive sensors: Since \(C = \kappa\varepsilon_0 A/d\), changes in \(d\), \(A\), or \(\kappa\) change \(C\). Applications: keyboard buttons (pressing reduces \(d\)), touchscreens (finger alters local \(C\)), accelerometers (movable plate shifts under acceleration), humidity sensors (water has \(\kappa \approx 80\)).

Filtering and timing: Capacitors smooth pulsating DC in power supplies and, combined with resistors, provide timing via \(\tau = RC\). We will study RC circuits in Chapter 27.

25.8 — Summary

Key Concepts

  1. Capacitance \(C = Q/\Delta V\) measures charge stored per volt — depends only on geometry and dielectric material. Unit: farad (F).

  2. Parallel-plate: \(C = \varepsilon_0 A/d\). Cylindrical/spherical capacitances depend on radii (Ch. 23–24 tools).

  3. Parallel: \(C_\text{eq} = C_1 + C_2 + \cdots\) (same \(\Delta V\), charges add). Series: \(1/C_\text{eq} = 1/C_1 + 1/C_2 + \cdots\) (same \(Q\), voltages add).

  4. Energy: \(U = \frac{1}{2}C(\Delta V)^2 = Q^2/(2C)\). Energy density: \(u_E = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2\).

  5. Dielectric increases \(C\) by factor \(\kappa\) via polarization. Dipole in field: \(\vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E}\), \(U = -\vec{p} \cdot \vec{E}\).

Key Equations

Quantity Equation
Capacitance \(C = Q/\Delta V\)
Parallel plate \(C = \varepsilon_0 A/d\)
Cylindrical \(C = \ell/[2k_e \ln(b/a)]\)
Spherical \(C = ab/[k_e(b-a)]\)
Isolated sphere \(C = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 a\)
Parallel combination \(C_\text{eq} = C_1 + C_2 + \cdots\)
Series combination \(1/C_\text{eq} = 1/C_1 + 1/C_2 + \cdots\)
Energy stored \(U = Q^2/(2C) = \frac{1}{2}C(\Delta V)^2 = \frac{1}{2}Q\Delta V\)
Energy density \(u_E = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^2\)
With dielectric \(C = \kappa\varepsilon_0 A/d\)
Dipole \(\vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E}\); \(U = -\vec{p} \cdot \vec{E}\)

Looking Ahead

In Chapter 26, we introduce electric current and resistance — charges in motion. We will discover Ohm’s Law (\(V = IR\)) and learn how resistance depends on material and geometry, much as capacitance does. Capacitor energy finds new purpose in RC circuits, where \(\tau = RC\) governs exponential charge and discharge.

*With capacitance, we complete electrostatics. Chapters 22–25 took us from charge to force to field to potential to energy storage. In Chapter 26, we set the charges in motion and enter the world of circuits.
